newsitem.title: USA: Oregon tax measures may hurt local credits - Moody's.
newsitem.headline: Oregon tax measures may hurt local credits - Moody's.

text.p: Two tax measures on the Oregon ballot could have severe credit implications for local governments in the state and may lead to rating downgrades, Moody's Investors Service Inc warned in its Credit Perspectives publication due out Friday.

On Nov 5, Oregon voters will consider ballot measures 46 and 47, the latest in a growing trends of anti-tax initiatives that could constrain the revenue raising abilities of municipalities and schools.
"Reduced financial flexibility, should it occur, might ultimately be reflected in lower bond ratings," Moody's stated.

The rating agency said the rising number and sweeping import of ballot initiatives may create a climate of greater uncertainty in the state's municipal market. This climate of uncertainty, Moody's warned, could increase borrowing costs for municipal issuers.
Measure 46 would alter the debt issuance process by redefining the voting majority to "all eligible" voters rather than, as it now stands, all those who "participate" in a vote.

Moody's said voter turnout is not generally high enough to achieve this approval rate. For this reason, passage of the measure could substantially reduce the likelihood that any tax or revenue measure submitted to the voters would be approved.

Moody's said the measure was designed to tighten the bond levy approval process for the issuance of unlimited tax, general obligation debt. Most affected would be tax base levies, special levies and the dedication of property taxes for future general obligation bonds, Moody's said.
The inability to obtain approval for tax levies would place additional strain on local governments in Oregon if off-setting cuts are not made, Moody's said.

Moody's said Measure 46 also contains retroactive language that may affect all voted debt issued after Nov 6, 1990. Moody's said that some issuers could be forced to pay debt service within existing operating tax limits, effectively converting the bonds into limited tax bonds.

Measure 47, by cutting property taxes and capping their increases, would reduce local government financial flexibility, Moody's said. The measure would uniformly affect general government entities and schools, regardless of tax rate limitations, by reducing taxes levied.

The measure would amend the Oregon Constitution to reduce property tax collections and to limit future annual increases in those taxes to three percent. The state Legislative Revenue Office estimates a 20 percent reduction in revenues for both schools and general governments as a result of this measure.

Measure 47 would also require the state Legislature to allocate property tax losses for local governments in a way that favors public safety and public education over other services. Moody's said portion of measure 47 are unclear and may be subject to debate if the measure is passed.
